__parsed_extra: Sibeprenlimab Reduced Proteinuria in Adults With IgA Nephropathy in Phase 3 VISIONARY Interim Analysis

An interim analysis of the VISIONARY phase 3 trial (containing adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy who were assigned 1:1 to sibeprenlimab 400 mg every 4 weeks or placebo, for 100 weeks) shows significant reduction of proteinuria in those patients given the trial drug sibeprenlimab. Sibeprenlimab targets APRIL, a B-cell–activating cytokine that promotes class switching and overproduction of Gd-IgA1 implicated in IgA nephropathy pathogenesis. Sibeprenlimab is currently under review by the US FDA for At 9 months, 24-hour UPCR fell 50.2% from baseline with sibeprenlimab and rose 2.1% with placebo; the adjusted geometric least-squares mean 24-hour UPCR was 51.2% lower with sibeprenlimab than placebo (96.5% CI, 42.9 to 58.2; P<0.001). At week 48, serum APRIL fell 95.8% and pathogenic galactose-deficient IgA1 fell 67.1% from baseline in the sibeprenlimab group. Safety was similar between groups; serious adverse events occurred in 3.5% of sibeprenlimab patients and 4.4% of placebo patients; no deaths were reported. The key secondary endpoint, annualized eGFR slope over 24 months, will be reported at trial completion. Sibeprenlimab is currently under review by the US FDA, and an approval decision is anticipated on November 28, 2025. More here: https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2512133

Atacicept Meets Primary Endpoint in ORIGIN 3 with Significant UPCR Reduction at Week 36

Vera Therapeutics reports that atacicept achieved the prespecified primary endpoint in the global, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 ORIGIN trial in adults with IgA nephropathy, with additional supportive biomarker and safety findings. Atacicept is a dual APRIL and BAFF inhibitor; these cytokines are believed to be central to the pathophysiology of IgA nephropathy. Atacicept reduced urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) by 46% from baseline and by 42% versus placebo at week 36 (p<0.0001). The treatment produced a 68% reduction in galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1). Hematuria resolved in 81% of participants who had hematuria at baseline. Overall adverse events were comparable to placebo, with fewer serious adverse events in the atacicept group and no deaths reported. UPDATE: Vera has submitted a Biologics License Application (BLA) through the Accelerated Approval Program to the U.S. FDA based on ORIGIN 3 data. The ongoing trial will continue to track 2-year eGFR data in 2027. Source: https://ir.veratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/vera-therapeutics-announces-positive-origin-phase-3-data
(Full paper at http://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2510198 for those who have a NEJM subscription.)

A UPCR of ~1.27 g/g is still pretty high and does put you at risk of further decline in kidney function, at least if you read the latest KDIGO guidelines. My understanding is that there are two separate issues with IgA nephropathy that need to be addressed. First is control over flares via IgA/Gd-IgA1 production. If you're getting povetacicept rather than a placebo, that could explain the ~67% reduction in proteinuria, which is inline with other data from this medication. But it also may be the case that you're getting a placebo, inflammation has died down (i.e. your flare has ended), and proteinuria has naturally fallen to this high number due to fibrosis. The second issue to address is managing CKD - reducing active inflammation and helping with other issues related to nephron loss, which you most definitely have with an eGFR of 23. I think the study allows for receiving an ACE inhibitor or ARB with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, but I may be mistaken. In your case, it seems like that standard of care isn't really doing the trick. I'd personally be pretty concerned remaining in a clinical trial with so much protein spillage still happening and an eGFR that low. Getting out of the trial just to be on sparsentan with an SGLT2 inhibitor (and using TRF-budesonide or sibeprenlimab to reduce IgA and Gd-IgA1 production) sounds like a decent way to at least preserve your kidney function for now. Have you talked with your nephrologist about all of this?

Biohaven Reports BHV-1400 Biomarker and Patient Data in IgA Nephropathy

Biohaven reports preliminary Phase 1b clinical biomarker and patient data for BHV-1400 in IgA nephropathy, including rapid galactose-deficient IgA1 reduction, early clinical observations, and competitor-positioning claims. BHV-1400 is a lead TRAP extracellular degrader designed to rapidly and selectively remove galactose-deficient IgA1, a theorized upstream driver of IgA nephropathy. BHV-1400 was reported to reduce galactose-deficient IgA1 by more than 60% within 48 hours in patients with IgA nephropathy, with reduction reaching 70% within one month of dosing. Biohaven stated that BHV-1400 produced deeper early galactose-deficient IgA1 reductions than those reported with BAFF/APRIL inhibitors, APRIL inhibitors, and CD38 inhibitors at early time points. The company reported associated observations during the one-month dosing period, including increased eGFR, decreased spot UPCR, and decreased hematuria. Biohaven reported no clinically significant reductions in total IgA, IgG, IgE, or IgM, and described BHV-1400 as selectively removing galactose-deficient IgA1 while sparing broader immunoglobulin levels. More here: https://ir.biohaven.com/news-releases/news-release-details/biohaven-reports-positive-clinical-biomarker-and-patient-data

IgA nephropathy is a progressive autoimmune disease, meaning that the damage to your kidneys accumulates over time. It's impossible to predict an individual person's IgA nephropathy trajectory with certainty because the disease presents so heterogeneously. That said, high proteinuria (>0.5 g/day, or even >0.3 g/day) is a strong indicator that an individual will progress to needing transplantation or dialysis. The medications you're on today - lisinopril, simvastatin, and dapagliflozin - in combination are relevant to the non-immunologic supportive-care component of IgA nephropathy; they aim to slow kidney function loss by reducing hemodynamic stress, proteinuria, and cardiovascular risk. You will likely be on these or something similar forever. Additionally, depending on where you are in the world, you will likely want to begin either TRF-budesonide or a new B-cell modifying agent, depending on what is available. These are relevant to the immunologic, upstream disease-production component of IgA nephropathy; they aim to reduce pathogenic IgA1 production and limit the immune-complex cascade that drives glomerular injury. The former is not yet approved for long-term use, and the latter can (and should) be taken indefinitely. Of course, you get to decide whether to start or continue any medication. But the data suggest that IgA nephropathy usually needs long-term treatment: supportive-care medications to reduce stress on the kidneys, plus disease-directed medications to limit ongoing injury and permanent damage.

Meds are of a for life thing. As others had mentioned since there is no cure the drugs are there to try to suppress the damage this disease can do to the body . Silbeprenlimab hasn’t been approved by EMA or MHRA yet.  Budesonide is available in UK and EU. It is a relatively new medication which is a corticosteroid that is designed in IgA medication to only target the part of your bowels that produce a lot of the IgA proteins that our bodies cannot remove. If you can tolerate it is quite an exciting drug therapy as it directly targets the disease. It is not a cure but the studies have shown positive results in both slowing down damage to the kidneys and reducing proteinuria significantly.  Another one that is approved in UK and EU is Sparsentan with the brand name Filspari. That is also specifically approved for IgA management. It helps with a lot of the downstream effects of IgAN. Including the proteinuria and high blood pressure if you have it.  At the moment they are generally being recommended for use in patients with high risk of rapid disease progression. So if your Renal Doctor suggests using it then it is sensible to take them.

That is all fairly standard first line treatment and lines up to what I was prescribed when diagnosed.  Lisinopril is a type of drug called an ACE Inhibitor which is primarily for treating high blood pressure, which is common in IgAN patients. This helps protect your kidneys and overall health. The clinical evidence also shows these drugs also protect your kidneys for longer.  Simvastatin helps reduce cholesterol levels in your blood, which helps protect our kidneys. And statins have further benefits to helping protect your kidney health.  Forxiga is a SGLT2 inhibitor which helps with reducing the pressure on your kidneys leading to help protect them, which also should reduce the amount of proteinuria you have.  All three are super important first line medications to help keep you healthy for longer. It is important to take them everyday consistently.
